6.14.m: Yudhiṣṭhira said: / “When Girijā was thus deluded by the illusory Maheśa, / what happened next, O holy one? Please tell me that.”
Nārada said: / “As Hari lay upon the Ocean of Milk, his heart was agitated; / suddenly, O king of kings, his eyes filled with tears.
Seeing that sign of a great portent, the Blessed Lord then / rose from Śeṣa’s couch, and looking at me and Vāyu,
Govinda, wondering what ought to be done, then remembered the enemy of the serpents. / And simply upon being remembered, he stood before the Lord with folded hands.
Seeing the son of Vinatā before him, Keśava said: / “O Suparṇa, go there where the battle is underway.
Has the hero Jālandhara been slain, or has Hara been deluded by him? / Having seen it, come back quickly and tell me everything.
You alone are capable of witnessing the battle between Jālandhara and the Lord; / what other embodied being, knowing of it, would go into that great combat?
Perhaps the battle there is impassable with showers of weapons and missiles; / so go, concealing your body, into the flight of arrows,
and observing Pārvatī's situation, you must return quickly.” / Reflecting hurriedly in order to dispel the demon's illusion, the Blessed Lord,
Hari, gave Garuḍa a pill that accomplishes everything: / “By this there will be no bewilderment, O hero!” Saying “So be it,” he placed it in his mouth.
Thus dispatched, the winged one circumambulated Hari, / departed, entered the sky, and flew with astonishing speed.
Having gone there, he saw the terrible battle, unbearable due to the hosts of Daityas; / he understood everything completely and indeed was not unaware of anything.
Flying up swiftly from there, he went to Mānasottara, / the loftier, impassable mountain, inaccessible even to the winds.
Looking around, the king of birds did not see Gaurī's abode; / having arrived there, the enemy of serpents indeed heard a sound.
Having gone near, he then saw the illusory Paśupati; / Garuḍa put the pill into his mouth and did not fall into delusion.
Having recognized and understood that this was a Daitya and not the bull-bannered [Śiva], / crying out, 'Alas, what misery!', and weeping, he went to the ocean.
He reported the account in the presence of the enemy of Kaiṭabha: / 'O Lord, Lord Hara has been mocked by Jālandhara;
Umā has been deceived by that evil one in disguised form. / If you are a god, O Govinda, go hence to battle;
wage illusory warfare against Jālandhara, O Lord of the gods! / His queen was seen by me in the auspicious seat of Jālandhara,
sporting on the palace grounds with the play of musical instruments, songs, and the like. / She is more beautiful than Gaurī, more than a hundred Rambhās and Urvaśīs;
now in the human world or in the nether worlds there is none equal to her. / As a wife, she is to be possessed by him; what talk is there of other women, O Hari?

Whoever touches her with his body becomes a fulfilled man. / And she is the wife of your brother-in-law; abduct her, O beloved of Ramā! / Render service to Śaṅkara and also secure your own happiness.'
Nārada said: / Having heard the words of Tārkṣya and rebuked him, the beloved of Ramā / rightly devised an expedient and quickly dismissed the bird.
Having deceived Śrī and covered her on the couch with a yellow garment, / he set out in another form by the power of a yogin's illusion.
Madhusūdana was infatuated by passion for the noble woman [Vṛndā]. / Seeing Hari departing in disguise, O Yudhiṣṭhira,
Śeṣa too, having approached Keśava in another form, / said with devotion: 'Remain; you should grant me permission.
What shall I do? Where shall I go? Tell me the duty, O Janārdana! / Always beholding your face I shall enjoy; so there may be happiness.'
The Blessed Lord said: / 'I shall abduct the lovely wife of Jālandhara for Hara's sake / and to render service to Pārvatī, having concealed my own body.
Come, brother, let us go to the impassable deep forest / to accomplish the attraction of Vṛndā.' Having spoken thus, the two went to the forest.
Then Viṣṇu and Śeṣa, wearing matted locks and bark garments, / founded a sacred hermitage that yields the fruit of all desires.
Their disciples and grand-disciples became shape-shifters: / lions, tigers, boars, bears, monkeys, and apes.
Then in that forest, Hari attracted Vṛndā with a mantra; / Madhusūdana caused intense anguish in her heart.
Meanwhile, the queen fell into severe affliction / and had fly-whisks waved, moved by the hands of celestial women.
Constantly thinking of the arrival of her beloved, the slender woman, / her limbs smeared with sandalwood and aloe, repeatedly fell into a swoon.
In the fourth watch of the night on the fourteenth [lunar day], the king's wife / saw a terrifying dream that indicated the terror of widowhood:
Jālandhara's dried head, smeared with pale ashes, / its eyes plucked out by a vulture, the tip of the nose and ears severed;
with disheveled hair, a dreadful face, dark in color, wearing red garments, / holding a skull-bowl in her hand, blood-mouthed Kālī was devouring it.
Such a dream she saw, and herself mocked likewise; / the king's wife saw [a portent] attended by the destruction of the Daityas.
Then the wife of the Asura king was awakened by the singing and playing of the bards, / by musical compositions, words of praise, and genealogical hymns recited by Kiṃpuruṣas.

Then, having given them all wealth born of favor since they were weary, / and having dismissed them, she summoned Brahmins and related the dream she had seen. / Having heard that dream, the Brahmins who had crossed to the end of the scriptures said to her:
The Brahmins said: / 'O queen, this very fierce nightmare is unfathomable and terrifying; / give gifts to the twice-born, for that destroys unfathomable fear.'
Cows, garments, jewels, elephants, and ornaments [she gave]; / completely satisfied, the Brahmins sprinkled the king's wife.
Even though consecrated, that Vṛndā was consumed by a fever; / having dismissed the excellent Brahmins, she then went to the palace.
Though staying there, she saw her own city as if its auspiciousness was blazed away. / Then, O king, she was drawn by Hari by virtue of his own deed.
She could not stay in the house; then the queen went to the forest, / having mounted a chariot yoked to she-mules, driven by her friend Smaradūtī.
Mounting it, in an instant the slender woman reached the Saubhāgya forest, / filled with various trees and endowed with flocks of various birds,
having streams of flowers, adorned by heavenly women, / where there was entrance only for the gentle breeze and for no one else.
Seeing the forest, the noble lady remembered her husband: / 'How shall I see the heroic Jālandhara arrived before me?'
Finding no pleasure there, she entered another forest, / accompanied by her friend and chariot, deluded by Viṣṇu's illusion.
Then the deer-eyed woman looked upon a forest dense with trees, / obstructed by huge stones, inspiring terror,
thronged with terrors of lions and tigers, frequented by jackals and serpents, / with trees whose crests touched the sky, filled with darkness in its caves.
Seeing the dreadful forest, trembling and with restless eyes, / Vṛndā spoke to her friend Smaradūtī, the driver of the chariot: / 'Drive my chariot quickly back toward home, O Smaradūtī!'
Smaradūtī said: / 'I do not know the direction, my friend; where shall I drive the chariot? / The mares are exhausted and there is no path here.
Driven by fate, let the chariot go wherever it will; / someone here, a flesh-eater, will surely devour us, not otherwise.'
Having been told this, she drove the chariot exceedingly fast; / moving swiftly, that chariot arrived where the Siddhas were, filled with joy.
There Siddhas were seen, and a terrifying forest, / where there was no strong wind, nor even the sound of birds,
nor was there bright light, nor water in any direction. / Even for the chariot that had arrived there, a reversal of signs occurred:
the she-mules did not neigh, nor was there any sound from the wheel-rims; / the banners did not flutter, and the small bells did not tinkle;
the great bells fastened to the flagstaffs did not sound. / Seeing such a state, Vṛndā said there to her friend:
'O Smaradūtī, where shall we go from this forest filled with the danger of tigers and lions? / There was no happiness for me at home in the kingdom, nor has any arisen in the forest, O friend.'
Smaradūtī said: / 'Listen, O queen! Behold, ahead is a very terrible mountain; / seeing it ahead, the mares do not advance, overwhelmed by fear.'
Hearing those words of hers, that king's wife was terrified; / seeing the necklace on her neck, she quickly rose from the chariot.
In the meantime, a demon of terrifying form arrived, / having three feet, five hands, and seven eyes, extremely dreadful.
He was tawny, with tiger-like ears, shoulders and face like a lion's; / his hair, resembling the king of birds, hung down, reddish like blood.
Seeing him, she whose body was like a lotus-calyx was suddenly terrified; / covering her eyes with both hands, she trembled like a plantain tree.
Abandoning the goad, the female gatekeeper spoke to the queen: / "Save me, frightened as I am, O queen; this one is running to devour [me]!"
In the meantime, the rākṣasa reached the vicinity of the chariot; / lifting the chariot with his hand, he whirled it along with its mares.
That queen fell to the ground like a doe from fear of a tiger, / and Smaradūtī at the foot of a tree like a broken aśoka creeper.
Then the rākṣasa devoured all those mares; / the queen was seized in his hand, like a young doe by a lion.
Then the rākṣasa said to her: "If you have any need for your life, / I have heard that your husband was killed in battle by Hari.

Take me as your husband today and live long, free from fear; / or drink delicious wine together with human flesh." / Hearing these words, the queen became as if lifeless.

Thus ends the fourteenth chapter, named 'The Narration of the Illusion of Glorious Mādhava,' in the story of Jālandhara, in the Uttarakhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa, in the collection of fifty-five thousand [verses].

6.15.m: Nārada said: / Then Lord Nārāyaṇa, wearing matted hair and bark garments, / arrived, accompanied by a second attendant carrying fruit in hand.
Seeing the two, Smaradūtī, deer-eyed, wept aloud. / Hearing her speech, both of them said to her:
"Do not fear, auspicious lady! We two have come to protect you. / Why have you entered a terrible forest infested by the wicked?"
Having thus comforted that slender woman, Mādhava said to the rākṣasa: / 'Release this woman of gentle limbs and charming smile, O you of vile conduct!'
O fool, evil-doer! What are you set upon doing? / You are preparing to make food of the very treasure of the world's eyes!
She is the power of the world's merit; will you slay this ornament of the earth? / Today you would make the world devoid of light and Kamdarpa devoid of pride,
if you now kill Vṛndārikā in the forest. / Therefore, quickly release this goddess of the palace of happiness!"
Hearing Hari's words, the rākṣasa, angered, said: / 'If you are capable, then free her right now from my hands!'
No sooner were these words spoken than, looked upon in anger by Mādhava, / he abandoned Vṛndā far off and fell down, reduced to ashes.
Then she, completely deluded by the illusion of the Lord of the Universe, said: / "Who are you, an ocean of compassion, by whom I have been protected here?
My bodily and mental suffering, full of anguish, O treasure of austerities, / has been removed by you with your sweet speech, through the destruction of the rākṣasa.
Gentle one, rich in austerities, I shall perform austerities in your hermitage."
The ascetic said: / "I am the son of Bharadvāja, renowned as Devaśarman. / Abandoning all enjoyments, I have come to the terrible forest
together with this young celibate, my disciple, moving at will; / and many others too are my disciples who take forms at will.
If, auspicious lady, you wish to perform austerities dwelling in my hermitage, / come, O queen, let us go to another forest, because it is located far off."
Having spoken thus to the king's wife, Hari went slowly / toward the eastern direction, to a forest filled with spirits and piśācas, O lord of men.
Vṛndārikā, her eyes filled with tears, followed behind him, / and Smaradūtī [came] behind her, saying, "Wait for me!"
In the meantime, some evil-doer of sinful appearance in the forest / cast a net; and when it was filled with living creatures,
then the lord of sin pulled that net tight; / then, having gathered the living creatures in the net, he released them.
And seeing the two women, the hunter said to Smaradūtī: / "Queen, he comes to devour me! Let my friend take me by the hand!"
Hearing what was said by her, Vṛndā looked at his deformed face; / seeing him, the beloved of the ocean-born shook, shaken by the wind of fear.
Overwhelmed, the fair one fled with Smaradūtī in the forest; / fleeing together with her friend, she came to the ascetic's hermitage.
In that ascetic forest, she saw an exceedingly great marvel: / birds with bodies made of gold, resounding with manifold cries.
She saw a pond filled with golden lotuses with golden banks; / rivers flowed with milk, and trees trickled with honey.
There were heaps of sugar, piles of sweetmeats, / all kinds of delicious foods, and many ornaments.
Many divine weapons fell from the sky, / and satisfied monkeys leaped, fell, and played.
In the hermitage Vṛndā saw that handsome ascetic, / seated on a tiger-skin seat, illuminating the three worlds.
She said to him: "O Lord, protect me, protect me from the wicked hunter! / Of what use are austerities, dharma, silence, and recitation?
There is no higher merit than protecting the frightened, O rich in austerities!" / Having spoken thus to the ascetic, she, frightened, her limbs languid—
meanwhile, that evil-minded binder of all living beings arrived. / Queen Vṛndā, terrified with fear, embraced Hari around the neck,
enjoying the pleasant touch with both arms, clinging like an aśoka vine. / "By virtue of your embrace, it will indeed be restored:
the head, endowed with all limbs, superior in virtues to your husband's. / Now, O beautiful woman, go to the picture-gallery for the sake of your husband."
Being thus addressed by the sage, she then entered the picture-gallery; / having climbed upon a divine couch and taken that head of her beloved,
with half-closed eyes, exceedingly lustful, she drank from his lower lip. / Meanwhile, O king, there appeared a form in the likeness of Jālandhara,
possessing a appearance like that of her beloved, his chest, an elevation like his, / his speech, and his mental disposition—then the Lord of the Universe became thus.
Then, seeing her beloved with a complete body, she said: / "I shall do what pleases you, my master! Tell me how you died in battle!"
Hearing Vṛndā's words, the illusory ocean-born one spoke: / "Listen, O queen, to how the battle took place between Śambhu and me.
Beloved, my head was severed by the terrible Rudra with his discus; / then, by the power of your perfection and by my spirit devoted to you,
severed though it was, it was brought here and revived by contact with your body. / Beloved child, you became grieved through separation from me.
Forgive the displeasure caused to me, that I left you and went to battle." / Then, by such words, Vṛndā was comforted by him,
and with betel, amusements, and beautiful clothes and ornaments. / Then the goddess Vṛndārikā, endowed with every enjoyment,
eager for amorous pleasure, embraced her beloved tightly and kissed him. / The bliss arising from the infatuation of Vṛndā, greater even than liberation,
Lord Nārāyaṇa considered superior to the essence of Lakṣmī's love. / While Mādhava dispelled Vṛndā's grief born of separation,
like a royal swan in a pond shining charmingly in their sport, / because of the disposition toward her form, Kṛṣṇa lost his desire for Padmā.
In that Vṛndāvana, she took the form of the tulasī plant; / from the sweat of Vṛndā's body, she manifested on the earth as exceedingly purifying.
Having experienced this happiness born of contact with Vṛndā's body / for some days, Hari, Lord of the Universe, remembered Śiva's business.
Once, at the end of sexual union, she saw on her neck / an ascetic, the two-armed Puruṣottama, clinging to her.
Seeing him, she released the embrace of her arms from his neck and said: / “How have you come in the form of an ascetic to deceive me?”
Hearing her words, Hari consoled her and said: / “Listen, O Vṛndārikā, know me to be the charmer of Lakṣmī.
Your husband has gone to defeat Hara and bring back Gaurī. / I am Śiva, and Śiva is I; we abide as distinct forms.
Jālandhara has been slain in battle; worship me now, O sinless one!” / Nārada said: / Hearing these words of Viṣṇu, her face became sorrowful. / Then, O king, Vṛndārikā angrily replied:
“He by whom you were bound in battle and released alive at your father’s word, / honored with various jewels—was it right to steal his wife?
How can the lord of dharma constantly delight in another’s wife? / The wise say that even the Lord experiences the fruit of action he has performed.
Just as I was led to delusion by you, an illusory ascetic, / so shall some illusory ascetic carry off your wife!”
Thus cursed, Viṣṇu vanished in an instant; / and that picture-gallery, the couch, and those monkeys also [vanished].
all vanished when Hari was gone. Seeing the forest empty, / Vṛndā went to her female friend and said, “Viṣṇu has acted deceitfully!
The city is abandoned, the kingdom is gone, my beloved's fate is in doubt; / finding myself in the forest, where shall I go, as ordained by fate?
The sight of my beloved has become a mere object of longing.” / Sighing hotly, Queen Vṛndā, exceedingly sorrowful, spoke:
“Death has indeed come upon me through you, O Smaradūtikā!” / Addressed thus by her, she replied, “You are my very life-breath!”
Hearing what she said, and then deciding in the forest what was to be done, / that Vṛndā went to a great lake there.
Casting aside her grief, she washed her limbs with water; / assuming the lotus posture on the bank and making her mind free of sense-objects,
she withered her own body, which had been defiled by contact with Viṣṇu. / She practiced severe austerities, taking no food, along with her friend.

Then a host of Apsarases, arriving at Vṛndā’s side from the world of the Gandharvas, / said: “Come, O auspicious one, to heaven! Do not discard your body!

'This is the Gāndharva weapon that conquers the three worlds, by which the Lord of Śrī was brought to the utmost satisfaction. / Why, O Vṛndā, do you discard this body here that has attained its desire?'

Know that your beloved was slain by an excellent arrow of the Trident-bearer; an ornament of celestial merit, / you must now quickly become [an ornament] of heaven, O passionate, auspicious one, and resort to the divine forest!”

Hearing the counsel of the women, the beloved of the ocean-born, laughing, spoke these words: / 'The wives of the lord of the thirty gods were brought from heaven and released by my exceedingly heroic husband.'

first I was the vessel of joys, and [he] conquered the immortals; now separated from that dearest one, unblemished, / I shall strive in such a way that I may reach my beloved who has attained immortality!”
Having spoken thus, Vṛndā dismissed the hosts of apsarases along with her companions; / bound by the cords of love for her, they constantly come and go.
Then, through the practice of yoga, having burnt the qualities with the fire of knowledge / and withdrawn her mind from the sense-objects, Vṛndā attained the Supreme.
Seeing Vṛndārikā there, the great hosts of Apsarases, / delighted, praised her from the sky and rained down showers of flowers.
Having made a pile of dry wood, placing Vṛndā’s body upon it / and kindling a fire, Smaradūtī entered it.
Taking the burnt body-dust of Vṛndā, which had formed into a ball, / and taking what remained of those ashes, they cast it into the Mandākinī.

Where Vṛndā abandoned her body and went along the path to Brahman, / there, near Govardhana, arose the Vṛndāvana forest.

Then the goddesses, having gone to heaven, proclaimed the excellence of the wife of the lord of the gods; / hearing that from the goddesses, all the immortals and others were delighted in their minds.
cast off their extremely powerful dread of their daitya enemy and sounded terrible kettledrums; / hearing that, the host of attendants sitting on their seats attained the splendor of good fortune.

6.16.m: Yudhiṣṭhira said: / How did Jālandhara, assuming the form of Hara, look upon Gaurī, O sage? / What did he do there? Tell me that in detail.
Nārada said: / When the illusory Śiva pleaded there with the Daughter of the Mountain, / she then became agitated, O king, and said nothing at all to him.
"This is improper for the untroubled god whom I attained through austerity"— / deciding thus, O king, Pārvatī did not speak to him.
Seeing no remedy there, and while he was watching, / she rose from that place, went out, and beheld the celestial river.
Deeming the Gaṅgā suitable for dwelling, Bhavānī went away for ascetic penance: / "Formerly too the Lord was obtained by me through penance; so it shall be now."
Pondering thus, she then went with her female companions, / [and saw] Pārvatī before her, resembling milk, high above in the sky, O king.
She then beheld the Mandākinī descending upon the Mānasottara mountain, / coming like a garland of pearl-necklaces, a pure garland of the sky.
The flood of water of the Mandākinī drawn from heaven was just like / the stream of the flood of the Vedas flowing from the mouth of Brahmā.
Seeing that Gaṅgā, she rejoiced; having bathed with her female companions / and then worshipped her own body, she sat down on the bank of the heavenly river.
Then, having looked at each other, Gaurī said to her friend Jayā: / "Go quickly near him, O friend, having assumed my form.
Find out the truth, whether he is Śambhu or if he will turn out to be someone else. / If he embraces you and bestows kisses and the like,
then know that an asura has arrived relying on illusion. / But if he should speak to you about good and bad regarding me,
he would undoubtedly be the Bearer of the Bow; come here and tell me." / Thus instructed by the goddess, Jayā went into the presence of the Bearer of the Gaṅgā.
Seeing her approaching, he, severely afflicted by love, / embraced her, imagining her in the form of Gaurī.
Thereupon, Jālandhara instantly discharged his semen, / and became instantly devoid of virility, O scion of the Kurus.
The daitya was addressed by her: "You cannot be Rudra, / you of little virility and base conduct! I am not Gaurī, but her friend!"
Having spoken thus and assuming her own form, she said to him again: / 'Alas, because of this sin you will indeed be slain by the bearer of the Pināka!'
Realizing this, she arrived, went there, and said to Umā: / 'O goddess, this is indeed Jālandhara, not Śambhu, your beloved.'
Then Hara's beloved became afflicted with fear and quickly entered inside a lotus; / the female friends became female bees within the lotuses out of fear of Jālandhara, O king.
Meanwhile, not seeing that royal lady who had gone to the forest, / her guards, terrified, quickly came to the battle.
Then, questioned by Śumbha, they bowed to him and, with trepidation, / spoke to Viṣṇu, that lord of the asuras, to exonerate themselves.
Hearing that Vṛndā had been abducted, terrified of Rudra and abandoning the battle, / Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa were dispatched by Śumbha to Jālandhara.
Having arrived at Mount Mānasottara at high speed, / the two Dānavas spoke to the Daitya, who wore the form of Hara, in the midst of the trees:
“O tiger among kings, what use is fortune gone to a foreign land, / which enemies do not see and which is not enjoyed by relatives?
Śumbha has been conquered and your army slain in battle by divine Rudra. / Come, come, wage war! You will not obtain Pārvatī.
How does a jackal obtain the lion's queenly consort? / O king, how does darkness reach the radiance of the sun?
From your seat of Jālandhara, your queen has been carried off by Murāri; / such news is reported, so wage war!
Conquer Śarva swiftly in battle and become the lord of all lords, / or else, shattered by Śiva's arrows, you will go to his abode.”
Hearing thus the speech of Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa, / Jālandhara departed from that mountain, enraged and red-eyed.
Having consoled Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa and cast off the form of Hara, / Jālandhara, going along the road, spoke to Durvāraṇa:
“Look, Durvāraṇa, at what Viṣṇu has done there now! / Resorting to illusion, Queen Vṛndā was taken to his own realm.
A wise man should never trust a son-in-law staying in his house; / indeed, having given him his daughter, a wise man should send him away.
A man should never establish a son-in-law in his own house; / bit by bit he takes everything: wealth, wife, and the rest.”

Durvāraṇa said: / “O king, whatever deed is done, just so its fruit is reaped: / you went to seize Gaurī, [so] your wife was seized by Hari.” / Hearing his blunt words, he remained silent for a moment and reflected.
Jālandhara said: / “Shall I march to conquer Hara, or violent Hari? / When two tasks arise, declare which is the higher!”
Durvāraṇa said: / “If you go to conquer Hari, Hara will strike from behind; / the heroes will slay in battle, and Rudra will not allow you to advance.
Therefore, having conquered Paśupati and brought him under your control, / march against Govinda afterwards, if you know his realm.
Now, O hero, go swiftly to the Daityas of great might; / wage a terrible battle, so that it may ripen well in heaven!”

Hearing Durvāraṇa's words, suited to the place and time, / Jālandhara then set out to fight with Rudra the Yogin.

in the Story of Jālandhara, the sixteenth chapter, entitled “The Renunciation of Jālandhara's Illusory Form.”

6.17.m: Nārada said: / Then Jālandhara saw the battle, terrifying with heaps of headless trunks, / impassable with floods of blood and flesh, marrow, fat, and bone.
There the Daitya Jālandhara, grieving over the abduction of his beloved, / beheld on the battlefield the lord of Pārvatī seated on his bull,

his limbs adorned with the coils of a terrible serpent, marked with the moon as an ornament in his matted hair, / his limbs radiant above the blaze of the fire of his eye: the ocean-born one saw him without any armor.
Quickly mounting his chariot, the son of the ocean then, / enraged, struck [his own arms] and said to Śumbha: “You did not kill the ascetic!”
Śumbha said to Jālandhara: “He has performed great asceticism; / Hara cannot be killed by us, he is invincible in battle.”
Hearing thus what was spoken by Śumbha, the ocean-born one, overcome with fury, / [marched against] Hara, accompanied by an army of Daityas comprising a thousand lotuses [of warriors].
Taking the bow named Kālakedāra, Jālandhara advanced; / sharp, massive arrows, as well as many iron shafts,
he loosed in the fight, difficult to overpower, like a cloud raining at the coming [of the monsoon]; / Śambhu's hosts blocked the advancing son of the ocean in battle.
Then he was struck in fury by Rudra with fierce volleys of arrows; / by Rudra's arrows, his armor was then cast down upon the earth.
Even without armor, he shone like a mountain free from clouds; / again Jālandhara's body was transfixed with arrows by Śambhu.
Copious blood flowed from Jālandhara's body; / by that flood of blood, the entire earth was swiftly inundated.
Then the gods took fright and the Dānavas trembled; / abandoning the battlefield, the heroic Pramathas fled.
An immense torrent, like a river, spread forth in all directions; / then the ocean-born one said to Rudra: “You are indeed the foremost of archers!
Now I shall do that by which you meet your end!” / Saying this, taking up the Kālakedāra bow with an arrow,
he swiftly covered Śiva with various kinds of arrows; / pierced in his limbs by thousands of crores [of arrows], Śiva shone in the battle,
like the sky filled with birds, or a great mountain with trees. / Seeing Maheśvara covered by those arrows loosed by the Daitya,
Vīrabhadra in wrath rushed against Jālandhara; / the mighty one of immeasurable soul afflicted the son of the ocean.
Then Jālandhara, intensely enraged, piercing with arrows by the thousands, / with his arrows reduced to sesame-sized pieces the bow, arrows, chariot, umbrella, and charioteer
of Vīrabhadra—the majestic son of the ocean did this. / Then Vīrabhadra, chariotless, struck the ocean-born one with his mace.
He too struck him in the same way with a mace and felled him to the ground; / seeing him fallen from the mace blow and utterly unconscious,
Maṇibhadra then charged at Jālandhara in the battle. / Seeing him advancing in extreme rage in that great fight,
the son of the river shattered his equipment with arrows; / then, casting off his swoon, roaring like a lion, he rose up.
Then from anger Vīrabhadra and the majestic Maṇibhadra, / the two of them struck the son of the river standing in the sky with two mountains.
Seeing the two mountains fallen on his body, having roared aloud, / Vīrabhadra struck the son of the river with a fist blow.
And Maṇibhadra, seizing the son of the ocean by the feet, / whirled him around from the chariot; it was as though a wondrous thing occurred.
Though grasped by Maṇibhadra, that mighty king of Daityas, / striking Maṇibhadra with a kick of his foot, brought him down,
and long-armed Jālandhara [struck] Vīrabhadra with his fist. / Then came the mountain-like Nandikeśvara with his attendants;
Seeing him arrive, Śumbha blocked him with his warriors; / then the Gaṇas and the Daityas engaged in single combats with one another.
Śumbha attacked the son of Śilāda; Rāhu attacked Mahākāla in the fight; / Niśumbha charged Kolāhala; Ketu attacked Kāla;
Śailodara attacked Guha; the mighty Jamba attacked Mālyavant; / Mahāpārśva marched against Caṇḍa; Caṇḍīśa against Romakaṇṭaka;
Vikaṭāsya against Bhṛṅgin; and Urunetra against Vināyaka. / Thus the leaders of the Gaṇas marched with the lords of the Daityas.
Then, struck by Śumbha's weapons and arrows, the monkey-faced son of Śilāda / smashed [Śumbha's chariot] with immense mountain peaks.
Afflicted by him, Śumbha struck the son of Śilāda with a spear; / then Mahākāla struck Rāhu at the forefront of the battle.
Then he struck his chariot with a spear and with a great mountain; / the powerful Kolāhala was struck with a spear by Niśumbha.
Taking a spear, he indeed struck the chariot together with the charioteer; / then by the daitya, deprived of his chariot and exceedingly enraged in battle,
Kolāhala was struck by the lord of the asuras with a thousand-hooded [weapon]; / and having struck him, he approached another chariot with great speed.
Struck by the serpent-missile in combat, abandoning unconsciousness within a moment, / quickly descending from his chariot and seizing sword and shield,
he cut into pieces everything belonging to Niśumbha, including his chariot and the rest, with his sword; / mounting his chariot again, he struck the daitya with arrows.
Niśumbha also, out of great wrath, astonished at his prowess, / being of great might, destroyed his chariot together with its horses by means of a spear.
Running into the battle, the mighty Kolāhala, though carless, / rushed at Niśumbha who was on a chariot, and rendered him chariotless by binding his arms.
And seizing the base of his standard, he whirled it in the sky; / and Kāla hurled a mountain, and he swiftly shattered the mountain.
Seeing that mountain crushed, he struck with his fist; / Kāla, with all his limbs crushed, fled in terror before the standard.
Likewise Śailodara struck Skanda on the chest with a mace; / the Six-faced One also, having struck him with his spear, brought him down to the ground.
Beholding the dānava dead from the blow of the spear, the Six-faced One / roared in marvelous fashion there, just as when Mount Krauñca was split asunder.
Then Mālyavān tormented Jambha in battle with floods of arrows; / Jambha also, having pierced him with sharp arrows, left him unconscious.
Mahāpārśva, checking his chariot deprived of horses by floods of arrows, / easily carried it off into the sky and cast down the horseless Caṇḍa.
Then, seeing his chariot horseless, Caṇḍa seized an elephant; / Caṇḍa struck with a mace Mahāpārśva who was rushing forward.
Disregarding the blow of the mace, that extremely fierce asura, / striking Caṇḍa with his fist, knocked him down to the surface of the earth.
Struck by the weapon of Caṇḍīśa, the great asura Romakaṇṭha / seized Caṇḍīśa by the feet and dashed him against the top of the chariot.
He fell suddenly to the ground; that fierce-eyed one went toward him. / Lambodara was struck with arrows in battle by Ūrunetra;
striking him on the chest with his tusk, he threw him down to the earth's surface. / Ūrunetra, recovering his composure within an instant, swiftly approached the chariot,
and struck with a mallet on his head adorned with vermilion; / the Lord of Gaṇas struck the dānava on the chest with a sharp spear.
Then from his mouth issued a great nine-headed asura; / he too, possessing eighteen arms, rushed toward the son of Śaṅkara, O king.
Vināyaka, blocked in battle by the nine-headed one and Ūrunetra, / though his body was mangled, seized his battle-axe in fury.
With that, the Lord of Gaṇas severed the weapons of both in the fight. / Then, seeing the Lord of Gaṇas blocked by both of them in battle, the Six-faced One,
the commander of the army, arrived swiftly and struck the nine-headed one; / having slain the nine-headed one in battle, he rushed toward Ūrunetra.
Skanda brought him down with the blow of his spear, O king. / Seeing this, Jālandhara advanced surrounded by his army against Skanda.
Out of affection for his son, Śaṅkara also went with his gaṇas to slay the asuras; / then a most terrible battle took place between the two wondrous armies.
In the battle between Hara and the ocean's son, heaven and earth seemed bereft of life. / Then Jālandhara, enraged, fitted a terrible arrow
adorned everywhere with feathers numbering hundreds of thousands; / with that arrow the lord of the daityas struck Śiva on the forehead.
It sank into Śaṅkara's forehead right up to the notch; / on Śambhu's brow the splendid king of arrows shone like the crescent moon,
just like the sun at the end of the hot season at twilight when the clouds arrive. / Then Rudra grasped a great arrow resembling a blazing fire.
In whose speed was the Wind, on whose tip were Fire and the Sun, / and Time was in all the joints: the Goddess who abides in the Earth was in that arrow.
With that arrow, Hara quickly pierced the ocean-born [asura] in the chest. / Struck by that arrow, drenched in a torrent of blood,
his limbs torn by the arrow, he fell like a mountain struck by a thunderbolt. / Then the daityas wailed, while the pramathas roared.
Seeing the ocean-born one unconscious, the dānavas blocked Śiva. / Some were intent on protecting him, while others stood around him.
While Jālaṃdhara, the son of the ocean, lay unconscious, / Rudra slew Jālaṃdhara's army with iron shafts.
At length, O king, Jālaṃdhara regained consciousness and saw his army slain, / and beholding the host scattered in the battle, he was filled with terror.
Then in his mind he remembered Kāvya, his supreme preceptor. / Remembered by him, the poet quickly arrived before Jālaṃdhara.
Having pronounced a blessing, the descendant of Bhṛgu said to the son of the ocean: / “O great king, what work may I do for you, O mighty one?”
Nārada said: / Hearing Kāvya's words, honoring the descendant of Bhṛgu, / and bowing to his preceptor, King Jālaṃdhara said:
The king said: / “Revive these dead daityas, O Śukra, all around!” / Thus addressed by the ocean-born, he looked upon the army there on the battlefield,
measuring twenty-five thousand yojanas, / strewn with the limbs of daityas and chariots, heaped one on another, O king,
heaped upon the earth to a height of ninety-five yojanas, / the ground there as if filled with the bodies of warriors and mounts.
And sprinkling them with consecrated water, the poet revived the daityas. / While Rudra was binding his matted hair firmly with serpents,
meanwhile, O king, that army was revived by Kāvya with a mantra, / like lions [springing upon] tigers, or lordly elephants [trampling] boars.
Seeing the dānavas returning, Śaṃkara reflected: / “What has happened here? Is someone somewhere generating the dead?”
As he reflected thus, Bhava saw Kāvya in that battle, / reviving the daityas in the conflict and rushing swiftly about.
Then the enraged Mahādeva resolved to kill Śukra. / But perceiving the trident-bearer, the poet said to him in secret:
“I am a brāhmaṇa, adept in all sciences; how can you kill me? / If I am killed, the sin of slaying a brāhmaṇa will be upon you, O Rudra.”
Hearing this speech of the poet, Śaṅkara cast away his trident, / remembering that previous event when Brahmā's head clung [to his hand].
[He thought:] “A brāhmaṇa must never be killed, even if he takes one's own dear life. / Yet this one, who revives the daityas, must be restrained by me by all means.
Therefore I will swiftly cast him into a female vulva, the reviver of daityas.” / When Śambhu had spoken thus, there quickly issued from his third eye
a Kṛtyā, naked and most fierce, with disheveled hair and a huge belly, / with large drooping breasts and vulva, terrible with fangs and eyes.
When she said to him, “Command me,” Śiva said to her: / “O Kṛtyā, throw the evil-minded preceptor of the dānavas into your vulva.
Hold him in your vagina until I slay Jālaṃdhara. / When the daitya Jālaṃdhara is slain, let him out afterward, crossing beyond.”
Told thus by Hara, that Kṛtyā ran toward the descendant of Bhṛgu. / Seeing her, the poet fell to the ground, and the daityas fled.
Pulling him by the hair, shaking him, embracing the naked Bhārgava, / that Kṛtyā placed him in her vulva, laughing, O delight of the victorious!
As the asura Jālaṃdhara saw his preceptor cast into the vulva / and aimed his arrows, that Kṛtyā vanished from sight.

6.18.m: The venerable Nārada said: / Then Jālaṃdhara said: “Protect yourself from me, O Śiva! / O Śiva, today I will swiftly cast you to where Madhusūdana dwells!
Afterward I will drag Brahmā and throw him into the ocean. / Once all of you are captured, I indeed will be the sovereign of all.”
Having said this, entrusting the gathering of the army to the asura Śumbha and others, / protected by Niśumbha and other warriors, an endless fourfold force,
Śumbha, Niśumbha, Pheṅkāra, Pheruṇḍa, Dhūmralocana, / Ketu, Biḍālajaṅgha, Rāhu, Durvāraṇa, Yama,
Kālāsura, then Lavaṇa, Bhūmiretas, Andhakāsura, / Raktavīrya and others, Caṇḍī and Cāmuṇḍī, bull-like daityas—
seeing all the bull-like dānavas ready in battle, / Vīrabhadra and the other gaṇas confronted them in the fray, O king.
Then a terrible, chaotic battle took place that made the hair stand on end, / in which the foremost daityas, afflicted by wounds, fell down.
Then, struck in the great battle by Śumbha and the other daityas with all kinds of weapons, / gaṇas fell, O king, while others took to flight.
Having conquered the gaṇas in battle, the dānavas blocked Śiva, / showering him with streams of arrows as clouds [shower] Mount Meru.

Then, drawing the Pināka, the terrible one upon the bull / struck down the dānavas on the battleground with hosts of arrows; / and the mighty one slew the dānavas with clouds of sharp-pointed crescent-headed shafts.
Some fell at the forefront of the battle from the blow of Nandin. / And having mangled Śumbha and the others with arrows, the bull-bannered god
swiftly destroyed the remaining army on the battleground with weapons and missiles. / Filled with fallen elephants, men, and horses, the field of battle
became like the surface of the earth covered with mountains shattered by a thunderbolt. / Then the ocean-born one created an illusory Gaurī.
Endowed with beauty and virtues, adorned with all ornaments, / having made an illusory Jayā, the son of the sea said to her:
“Go quickly before Rudra in the battle and bewilder him.” / Having been spoken to thus by the lord of daityas, the illusory Jayā went.
Having gone into the battle before Śiva, she wept with disheveled hair. / Questioned by Hara, she said: “From Mount Mānasottara,
your beloved Pārvatī has been abducted by the son of the ocean, O god!” / Hearing these words of hers, the bull-bannered god said to her:
“O Jayā, come to the bull! The dānavas will seize you.” / Then, mounting the bull, Jayā embraced Śaṃkara,
and said: “I depart with Pārvatī; I will not live without her, O Hara!” / Quickly taking the moon nestled in Śambhu's matted hair, from the bull
she dismounted, that phantom woman, and went to the battle. / Then, hearing that Gaurī had been abducted, Śaṃkara grew anxious;
clasped in the daitya's illusion, he did not know himself, O king. / In the meantime, surrounded by a vast army, there arrived
the ocean-born [demon] before Śiva, having placed an illusory Mṛḍānī upon his chariot. / There arose the roar of instruments, such as “Victory to Jālaṃdhara!”
by which the earth trembled and the mountains resounded. / The son of the ocean showed Pārvatī to Hara.
Rudra, too, saw his own beloved standing in his enemy's chariot, / distressed by separation, wretched, slender, with agonized eyes,
wailing repeatedly, “Alas, my lord! Dear Rudra!” / seeing her on the arrogant enemy's chariot like the Śruti in the hands of a heretic.
Then Sthāṇu brooded over Gaurī: “How can my beloved be regained by me?” / Deluded by the demon’s illusion, Śambhu then lamented:
“Deluded by the Dānavas, my lovely one, you have been abducted! How, my beloved?” / Seeing Śaṅkara overwhelmed by sorrow and delusion, the ocean's son,
laughing aloud, spoke a speech as if someone possessed of compassion: / “You are void of all authority, stripped of erotic desire and love!
Even though you are the Lord, you have become a wretch without Ambikā! / Do not weep, O Virūpākṣa, I give you your beloved!
You have been protected by me, O Rudra, taking Pārvatī from the battle!” / Having spoken thus to the mountain-dweller, swiftly bringing Umā down from his chariot,
he dispatched an army directly toward Śaṅkara. / Hara too quickly rushed on his bull toward that army,
to seize Pārvatī, who was crying, “Protect me, save me, save me!” / Just as the bull-bannered lord reached out with his hand to seize that Gaurī,
at that moment the asura Śumbha swiftly seized her and stood in the sky. / Hara, mighty as he was, hurled his trident to slay the asura Śumbha.
Abandoned by Śumbha, she fell onto the trident; / weeping, fair-limbed all over, released, she was pierced through by the trident.
She fell before Śaṅkara and died, saying, “So be it.” / Seeing the illusory Gaurī dead, overwhelmed by sorrow and delusion,
crying, “Ah, beloved!” Rudra fell unconscious to the ground. / Then, regaining consciousness for a moment on the battlefield, the lord of Umā / cursed Śumbha and the others: “Gaurī shall slay you!”
Nārada said: / Then Śumbha and the other demons were struck down in battle by the goddess / through the curse of Maheśvara when a manvantara had elapsed, O king.
Having cursed them, Śaṅkara then went out and wept, crying out: / “Where have you gone, my beloved, leaving me sorrowful on the field of battle?
I, Śrīkaṇṭha, have been deprived of pleasure and afflicted with separation by you! / Even Vāsudeva does not know that I have been abandoned by you, my beloved!
At the sacrifice of Dakṣa, O goddess, your head was offered into the fire pit. / You were regained again by me; why do you abandon me once more?
Arise, arise, O fair-limbed daughter of the mountain, speak to me!” / Meanwhile, realizing that Śiva was deluded by the demon's illusion,
the lotus-seated [Brahmā], situated among the assembly of gods, came down from the sky / and, invisible, spoke thus to the lamenting one:

Brahmā said: / “You are free from sorrow, delusion, father, and mother; you have neither pain nor pleasure, son, wife, nor enemy. / You were never born from a father, nor are you about to be born; you are praised by the hosts of sages: whence this delusion?

You are one, O Lord, and you assume many forms, like the sun seen in the waves of the ocean. / By meditation the self-restrained reach the base of your feet; your supreme form is incomprehensible and inexpressible indeed!

This is not your beloved who has perished in such a manner; cast off the illusion crafted by Jālandhara, O god! / That Pārvatī is within the calyx of a lotus, O Śambhu; fight, slay the host of your enemies, and protect us!”
Having heard these words of Brahmā, Maheśvara was awakened to the truth. / Recognizing that demonic illusion, he hurled a massive rock.
With it he slew three hundred million demons in battle. / Then, mounting his bull with great fury, O king,
Dhūrjaṭi grasped his bow Pināka and arrows for battle. / Then, seeing Śarva free from the illusion, the ocean-born one,
in order to delude the lord of the gods, O king, swiftly manifested another / exceedingly wondrous web of illusion, exceedingly mighty in power.
Jālandhara became ten-million-armed and fought the bull-emblemed lord with trees, missiles, and weapons. / Then in between, the son of the ocean made the earth adorned with mountain minerals,
and the son of the ocean adorned the earth, O king, with delightful shrines of the gods / filled with various flowers, where apsarases like Menakā danced charmingly.

Forgetting [the battle], Śambhu cast aside his bow and at once set out, mounted upon his bull; / he was greatly enchanted on the earth by the instruments, songs, and the tāṇḍava dance conjured by the demon lord's illusion.

Beholding Hara seated upon the bull continually deluded along with the tāṇḍava, / the ocean [demon] assumed forms with song, instrumental music, and playful dance, roaring loudly to delude him with haste.
Having cast thousands of creatures into the ocean, he celebrated a perpetual festival. / Where were all those gods? Where were the gaṇas headed by Nandin?
“Even you, who are worthy of honor, are deluded by the demon's illusion! / Why, O holy Śambhu, do you neglect this today? Dispatch the discus resting in your belly,
which was made for the destruction of this very one, O Maheśa, and slay Jālandhara with it in battle!” / At these words of Kṛṣṇa, remembering himself to be the Lord,
he quickly mounted his bull and arrived at the great battle. / Seeing that Śiva had arrived, surrounded by his entire army,
the angry asura Jālandhara confronted him in battle, O king. / For the enraged Hara there appeared the form that brings about the destruction of creation,
like the fire of the third eye, and the Dānavas were like moths [before it]. / Seeing that form of the Lord consisting of fierce flames, O king,
the demons such as Śumbha, and those headed by Rāhu, / terrified upon seeing Rudra, entered the netherworld out of fear.
Seeing his numerous warriors slain in the great battle, / and seeing those who survived, such as Śumbha, fleeing,
Jālandhara then stood alone in the conflict like a mountain, / delighted, beholding the true reality of Rudra's form before his very eyes.
Then Jālandhara laughed and spoke to Mahādeva: / “Withdraw the form by which you burn the moving and unmoving universe!
Wage battle with weapons, abandoning your power of yoga!” / Hearing these words of Jālandhara, Śiva then spoke:
“Choose a boon, O lord of demons! I am pleased with your deed, / since even upon seeing such a form of mine you are now fearless!
Even the entire universe is overwhelmed merely by the sight of the splendor / of this form of mine, O Dānava, yet there you stand fearless!”
Nārada said: / Thus considering Śambhu's favor and indifferent to worldly existence, / Jālandhara chose from Hara liberation, the supreme union [with him].
The auspicious Mahādeva said: / “This divine body of yours, endowed with the attainment of pleasures, / charming to Vṛndā and delightful, enjoys time while dwelling here.
Without knowing that solitary, imperishable supreme self even for a moment, / you cast it aside, O fool! How do you desire liberation?
Your beloved queen Vṛndā was taken away by yogamāyā; / having realized the nature of Brahman, she attained that supreme state.
Now she is difficult to attain, and that state too is difficult to attain. / Choose a boon within worldly existence, between heaven and final release!”
Jālandhara said: / “O God, the state of the liberated is to be gained by one who has accomplished his duty. / I am now one who has accomplished his duty, since I behold you and will be slain by you.”
Śiva said: / “If you are eager to go to my supreme realm and sacred field, / then quickly enrage me by striking the demon with firm arrows.
Then I shall strike you down, and you will go to my realm, O sinless one.” / Hearing the words of Maheśvara, Jālandhara said to Śiva:
“I will not strike first against you, who are worthy of worship by the entire world!”
Nārada said: / Addressed in this way, Śiva swiftly struck the ocean-born [demon] with arrows. / Those arrows, clinging to the body of the ocean's son, shone forth,
like bamboos kindled by fire on the slope of an iron mountain. / Jālandhara covered the body of Hara with arrows.
Rudra shone with those arrows, as the sky is filled with birds; / O king, such was the duel that took place between Jālandhara and the Lord.
None other than Hara was his slayer, nor could anyone else bear [the attack] from the ocean's son. / Then, with ten million mountain peaks uprooted from the earth's surface,
the ocean-born [demon] showered the husband of Pārvatī in battle. / Then, struck in the chest with a trident by Rudra, the Dānava
let forth from his mouth a terrifying, yawning fever. / And that fever was called Vīrajvara, lion-faced and human in form.
Seeing that lion-faced fever emerge from the Daitya's body, / [Śiva] let out a dreadful shout, and there emerged a Śarabha.
Struck down by that Śarabha that issued from Śiva, [the fever was felled]. / Seeing Śaṃkara invincible, accompanied by the lord of bulls,
the son of the ocean swiftly advanced into the presence of the bull. / Seizing the bull by the tail, he swung it about in the sky,
and the mighty-armed Jālandhara hurled it onto the Himavat mountain. / Then the husband of the mountain-born goddess released his exceedingly fierce trident.
Seizing it with his hand right before Śiva, / the lord of Daityas, born of the ocean, mounted his chariot, took his bow,

and covered Śiva, who stood on the surface of the earth, with arrows on the Kālakedāra [battlefield]. / The fierce [Śiva], cutting down his weapons and arrows with his own shafts, smashed the chariot,
ten yojanas wide, together with its charioteer and horses. / Even though deprived of his chariot, Jālandhara charged at Śiva in the battle.
Between the two there was a dreadful, wondrous fight that made the hair stand on end. / Seeing it, the gods were terrified, fearing an untimely dissolution of the cosmic age.
They of terrible prowess struck each other with all their missiles, / shaking the earth and the like with their feet, and making the sky tremble with their roars.
Then, seeing the immense strength of the lord of Dānavas, / Śaṃkara swiftly stripped away his array of weapons by the power of his yogamāyā.
Then the Daitya, possessing ten million arms, with terrifying fangs and eyes, / though bereft of weapons, rushed swiftly and went towards Hara.
With a clasp of his vast hands, he bound Śiva in battle. / Then, with a sword, [Śiva] severed that forest of hands.
Overwhelmed by the arms of the ocean-born one, Rudra became blue-and-red. / That son of the ocean fought in the battle as if in play.
Though his arms were cut off, he fought on, like Svarbhānu with [only] his head. / With close-quarters combat, the son of the river pleased Śaṃkara.
Highly pleased, Śambhu said: “Choose a boon difficult to obtain.” / Jālandhara said to him: “Give me your own position.
You ought not to show contempt for me, [merely] because I am deprived of arms and weapons. / Grant me success quickly, or else I will destroy you.”
Having spoken thus, having assumed arms, he struck him on the chest with his fist; / then the Sudarśana discus, which had been fashioned in the past by [Śiva] himself,
Disgorging it from his mouth, he seized it in his hand and balanced it in wrath— / blazing like a thousand crore suns, swallowing the moving and unmoving world.
With that discus, he severed the head of Jālandhara. / Then that head leaped up a hundred yojanas into the sky,
with a terrifying mouth possessing hundreds of fangs, its eyes turned toward the sky and the earth; / and then, O king, with the stride of a tiger, it went to the abode of Brahmā.
Seeing it again in heaven, Mṛḍa ran after the head, / while it streamed copious blood and made a dreadful sound.
Then the quarters vanished, the sky dissolved away, / there was no light of luminaries, and the earth trembled out of fear.
Rudra quickly struck down that rushing head with his discus. / Cleaved into two, O lord of kings, it fell upon the Himavat mountain.
Then, indeed, both parts of Jālandhara's head / entered into Vṛṣākapi before the eyes of all beings.
From his neck arose hundreds of thousands of Daityas; / they were slain by that discus shining in the hand of the matted-haired Lord.
The headless trunk of Jālandhara danced, red with blood. / Again and again, Dānavas arose from his neck,
and again and again they were cut down by the mighty Śambhu with his discus. / The entire earth was filled with the fat of the ocean's son;
hence, O king, it gained the name Medinī, from fat alone. / Where the blood of this foremost Daitya turned into a mountain,
there, on the northern side of Kailāsa, arose the city of Śoṇitapura. / Then, seeing the heaps of flesh remaining spread out everywhere,
the lord of the gods remembered in the battle the sixty-four attendants. / By his mental recollection, the goddesses arrived at the presence of Śaṃkara.
With folded hands, they said: “Śiva, what shall we do?”
Mahādeva said: / “These heaps of Daitya flesh resemble mountains; / quickly devour them together, for my permission is granted to you.”
Brāhmī, Māheśvarī, Kaumārī, Vaiṣṇavī, / Vārāhī, and Māhendrī—all adorned with their respective retinues,
directed in this way by Śaṃkara, the goddesses, beholding those piles of flesh / with cruel eyes, made them vanish in an instant.
Then the body of Jālandhara was consumed and overwhelmed by the Śaktis. / When his body had been swallowed by them, from his corpse there emerged
a brilliance; it reached Śaṃkara and vanished in an instant. / That splendor, resembling the sun, attained dissolution into Maheśvara.
Thus that enemy of the gods met his dissolution through the three-eyed Lord. / Pleased, Maheśvara said: “All of you, choose a boon.”
Then all those yoginīs asked the Lord of the universe: / “In the mortal worlds, those people who desire the boon of enjoyment and liberation,
and who will worship the troop of yoginīs constantly in their homes— / may all that they desire be accomplished by your grace.”
Mahādeva said: / “Whoever constantly worships your troop with a devotional disposition, / to him on the surface of the earth I shall grant boons.
Even if he is a devotee of mine or of Keśava, if he hates the troop of yoginīs, / then, becoming Bhairava, I will take away whatever merit he has performed.”
Having been thus granted boons by the Lord in battle, the Yoginīs were delighted; / in the meantime, Hara remembered Bhavānī and that bull.
As soon as she was remembered, Pārvatī and the bull arrived in an instant; / accompanied by her circle of female companions, the beloved of Hara arrived.
Casting off her form as a bee, she mounted half of Hara's body. / Joined with the daughter of the mountain, O king, Maheśa then rejoiced.
He said to the yoginīs: “Drink the blood / residing in the headless trunk of Jālandhara, O king!” Hearing that, they rejoiced greatly.
Having drunk the flesh, fat, and blood, the yoginīs danced with joy. / Then Hara was pleased by witnessing their play.
Assuming a Bhairava form himself, he stood in their midst and drank. / The hosts of yoginīs were then sharp-fanged and immense in body.
Devouring the meats even now, they also drink blood in due season. / Because of this, the slain Daitya Jālandhara does not rise again in battle.
Then the hosts of deities headed by Brahmā arrived there; / the sages, Maruts, and gods praised Maheśvara.

The directions grew clear, fragrant winds blew, and showers of flowers fell from the sky upon the earth; / and they caused kettle-drums to resound, making sounds for him whose consecration was accomplished.

Carried heavily above by swarms of bees flying together with pleasant buzzing, blinded by the fragrance, / soaking the earth with unbroken streams and showers of honey, a shower of flowers released by the gods fell upon the assembly.

When the son of the ocean was slain at that time by Hari with blows of arrows, the three worlds then shone forth; / there was a shower of flowers, women danced, and Yakṣas, gods, and Kinnaras sang.

Śambhu, his renown and body vast with the fame arising from the victory over his enemy, / returned to his mountain, constantly praised by hosts of gods, Siddhas, and Cāraṇas.

Gaurī too quickly departed from the white mountain, surrounded by her companions; / and divine maidens rendered service with a shower of flowers.

That merciful god, restoring the hosts of gods to their respective posts, / granted further wealth of his own, and Śaṅkara was then acknowledged as the Lord.
What more need be said beyond this? If the supreme compassion of the Lord be present, / what is this heaven or this earth? Everything becomes his own.
Having attained their own kingdoms, the gods shone as before; / taking their place as guardians of the world, they enjoyed their sacrificial portions.
Nārada said: / Thus, O king, has the wondrous deed of Jālandhara, / the hero of the worlds, been narrated to you properly and in order.
Even today Viṣṇu does not abandon the ocean of milk, subjugated by which [power of karma], O king; / everyone reaps the fruit of their own karma; know that to be karma without a doubt.
This supreme narrative has been spoken to you for the dispel of your grief; / as long as there is a body, there is karma, and pleasure and pain arise from karma.
The embodied soul experiences them helplessly, O king; there is no protection higher than knowledge. / In the embodiment of Kṛṣṇa and others, pleasure, pain, and the like exist.
What then can be said of others, who have turned away from dispassion? / Knowing such to be the course of karma, stronger than all else,
be steadfast; await the return of auspicious karma. / Having conquered your enemies in due time, you will regain your own kingdom.
Having heard this legendary history, one is not overcome by sorrows; / and here dharma, wealth, pleasure, and liberation are duly proclaimed.
It leads to heaven, removes sins, brings merit, and destroys grief and delusion. / A brāhmaṇa attains knowledge; a kṣatriya attains a kingdom;
a vaiśya attains abundant wealth; and a śūdra attains happiness upon hearing it. / A king, even if fallen from his kingdom, by remaining devoted to the good path,
regains that kingdom through constantly hearing this [narrative]. / O king, having heard this, good people relish nothing else to listen to,
just as the sweet melody of a cuckoo [makes pleasing], while the cry of a crow seems harsh. / Having heard this sinless narrative, a lover of the heart of good people
should gratify the reciter with gifts of gold, sesame, cloth, cows, and land; / and when he is pleased, one obtains the fruit.
The deities are pleased when the reciter-guru is honored; / and one should give gifts of food and worship brāhmaṇas.
Whoever hears this supreme narrative constantly becomes victorious, / endowed with sons and grandsons, and is born in the realm of Viṣṇu.
O king, those best of men who hear, under this pretext, / the origin of Tulasī, are never tainted by sin.
This glorification of tulasī is sacred and destroys sins; / having heard it and recited it, one attains liberation—there is no doubt.
And tulasī planted in one's own house destroys sins; / even the sin of killing a brāhmaṇa is destroyed merely by seeing it—there is no doubt here.

In Kārtika and in Māgha, one should worship Hari with tulasī; / and worship of Hari in Vaiśākha is remembered to be especially auspicious.

By a single circumambulation indeed, all sin is destroyed forever; / those Śūdras on earth who are devoted to giving gifts attain purification in time.
even their bodies become worthy of worshipping the gods, and they have gone far from sin; / indeed, devotees of Viṣṇu are exceedingly rare in this Kali age nowadays.

6.19.m: Yudhiṣṭhira said: / O Nārada, where does the charming mountain Śrīśaila stand? / What sacred bath is there? Worship of which god? / In which direction is it declared to be among the worlds? Tell me now.
Nārada said: / Listen, O king, I will describe Śrīśaila, the best of mountains, / hearing about which a person is freed from sins such as child-murder.
The charming forest on that mountain is resorted to by sages, / filled with various trees and creepers, and adorned with various flowers.
It echoes with the cries of swans and cuckoos, and the cries of peacocks; / with śrī trees, kapittha, śirīṣa, and rājavṛkṣa trees;
with pārijāta blossoms, and likewise kadamba and udumbara trees; / perfumed with various flowers rich in fragrance, that forest stands on the mountain.
It is well-served by all the sages' wives together with their disciples. / Some are engaged in study, and some are devoted to exposition;
some stand there with upraised arms, others on the tips of their big toes; / some are devoted to meditation on Śiva, and some are dedicated to Viṣṇu.
Some here are fasting, and some are devoted to eating dry leaves; / some eat roots and fruits, while some maintain the vow of silence.
Some stand on one foot, others remain in the lotus posture; / and some, fasting, perform severe austerities difficult to accomplish.
There are sacred hermitages and various auspicious rivers, / numerous divine pools and many ponds.
This mountain, O great king, is seen indeed on all sides, / where Mallikārjuna constantly resides, O king.
And that charming peak frequented atop the mountain— / merely by seeing that peak, liberation is attained; there is no doubt.
This best of mountains stands facing the southern direction. / Here the great, charming Gaṅgā reaches as far as the netherworld.
Merely by bathing there, one is freed from great sins. / Having seen the peak of Śrīśaila, one's death is certainly as if in Vārāṇasī.
And having drunk the water at Kedāra, there is no rebirth. / It is a great place for ascetics, and likewise for yogins.
Therefore, by every effort, one should obtain a sight of it. / This god of knowledge destroys great sins.
And Siddhāpura is a charming city that brings the happiness of heaven, / where apsarases constantly sing and sport.
Hence this king of mountains causes happiness upon sight. / Those people who desire liberation should behold it.

6.20.m: Glorious Mahādeva said: / Listen to [the glorification of] Haridvāra, of great merit, O best of divine sages, / where the Gaṅgā flows; it is declared to be the best of sacred sites.
Where gods reside here, and likewise sages and Manus; / where the god Keśava himself is directly and constantly present.
Formerly in ancient times, my child, that great pilgrimage place came to be, / merely by the sight of which sin departs far away,
where the most delightful Gaṅgā became exceedingly sacred, / having become water from the feet of Viṣṇu, because of touching his feet.
O learned one, she was brought along that path by Bhagīratha, / and the salvation of his ancestors was accomplished by that great-souled one.
Nārada said: / Who is this Bhagīratha of great austerities declared to be, / by whom the holy pilgrimage place was brought for the welfare of the worlds?
The Gaṅgā pilgrimage place is of great merit and destroys all sins; / all people indeed proclaim this to be the highest of the highest pilgrimage places.
Whoever says ‘Gaṅgā, Gaṅgā,’ even from hundreds of leagues away, / is freed from all sins and goes to the realm of Viṣṇu.
How was she brought by him, and what deed was done? Tell me, O one of noble vows. / Mahādeva said: / By whom and how the Gaṅgā was brought to most splendid Gaṅgādvāra,
all that I shall declare in proper succession. / Formerly there was Hariścandra, who maintained truth in the three worlds.
Rohita was his only son, devoted to Viṣṇu. / His son was Vṛka, most righteous and standing on the path of truth.
His son was Subāhu, born at that time in this lineage. / His son was named Gara, who was exceedingly righteous.
Once, due to the course of time, he became distressed because of a calamity there; / but the king was threatened in that land for the sake of dharma.
Taking his family, he went to the hermitage of Bhārgava; / then he was protected there out of compassion by the Bhārgava at that time.
There indeed a son was born to him named Sagara, O twice-born; / and he grew up in the holy hermitage, protected by the Bhārgava.
All the rites of a kṣatriya, such as the sacred thread, were performed then, / as well as practice with weapons and the Vedas likewise.
Then King Sagara, having obtained the fire-weapon from the Bhārgava, / traversed the earth and struck down the Tālajaṅghas along with the Haihayas.
That man of great austerities slew the Śakas and the Pāradas. / Nārada said: / O Śaṅkara, tell in detail the greatness of Sagara.
Mahādeva said: / He was a celebrated and mighty emperor of the Solar dynasty; / when Gara met with misfortune, my dear, his kingdom was indeed seized
Along with the Haihayas, the Tālajaṅghas and others, and the Śakas, O Nārada, / the Yavanas, the Pāradas, the Kāmbojas, and likewise the Pahlavas,
These five groups, O brāhmaṇa, through their valour on behalf of the Haihayas [seized it]. / Then the king, his realm having been seized, Sagara, went into the forest.
Followed by his wife, distressed, he gave up his life-breaths. / His wife, auspicious and pregnant, was dedicated to vows.
The Bhārgava had formerly been chosen by that co-wife desiring a son. / She, having prepared her husband’s funeral pyre, wept loudly in the forest.
Aurva, having restrained her, the wife of Gara, O Nārada, / announced to her a son: righteous, sattvic, and beloved.
When the child was thus announced, she desisted from death; / then, two months having elapsed, he was born and grew up in Aurva's hermitage.
The rites such as the birth rite were performed by Aurva; / all rites such as the investiture with the sacred thread were performed there by the great sage.
There all the Vedas and other texts were studied under Aurva's guidance. / Having taught the Vedas and treatises, he then imparted weapons to him,
the fiery weapon, O fortunate one, unbearable even to the immortals. / Endowed with that weapon of swift might and with personal strength,
infuriated, he swiftly slew the Haihayas with his own army. / He subdued them in the worlds and attained renown.
Then the Śakas, together with the Yavanas, Kāmbojas, and Pallavas, / being slaughtered then, went to Vasiṣṭha for refuge.
Vasiṣṭha too, having bound them by a covenant, of great splendour, / restrained Sagara, having granted them freedom from fear, O king.
Hearing his own pledge and the words of his guru, / Sagara struck them in accordance with lawful ways and disfigured them.
He shaved half the head of the Śakas and dismissed them; / the whole head of the Yavanas, and likewise of the Kāmbojas;
the Pāradas were made to have loose hair, and the Pallavas made to keep their beards. / Thus having conquered all of them, he established the order of dharma.
The king, victorious over all dharmas, having conquered this earth, / swiftly made preparations for a horse sacrifice, the ruler of the earth.
As he let it wander, that horse in the southeast ocean, / near the shore, was carried away and made to enter the earth.
He then had that region dug up everywhere by his sons. / They did not find the horse then, as the great ocean was being excavated.
There, filled with haste, they saw the primeval person; / they [saw] that god, the primeval person, Kapila, the lord of the worlds.
By the fire arising from his eyes as he woke up, / the sixty thousand were burnt; only four of them remained:
Hṛṣīketu, Suketu, another named Dharmaratha, / and the valiant Pañcajana, founders of his lineage, O twice-born.
And the Lord Hari himself granted him five boons: / continuation of his line, liberation, fair renown, and the ocean as his son, the omnipresent Lord.

And [the ocean] attained the status of 'sāgara' by that deed of his. / He retrieved that sacrificial horse from the ocean; / and that king of great renown performed a hundred horse sacrifices.

Nārada said: / How were the heroic, mighty sons of Sagara born, / the sixty thousand valiant ones? Tell that, O lord of supreme knowledge.

The lord of Pārvatī said: / Sagara had two wives whose sins were burnt away by asceticism. / Aurva, the best of sages, being pleased, granted a boon to the two.

One chose sixty thousand energetic sons; / the other, endowed with boons, chose one sole continuer of the lineage, as she desired.

There, one gave birth to a gourd containing many heroic sons; / all of them were raised in due order by foster-mothers

in jars filled with clarified butter, the boys increasing delight, / [nourished] with the milk of brown cows there for those noble ones.

By means of that very milk they grew, those great-souled ones. / One, named Pañcajana, became a king and son.

From Pañcajana was born the powerful one named Aṃśumān; / his son was Dilīpa, whose son was Bhagīratha,

Nārada said: / How was the Gaṅgā brought, and what austerity was performed by him? / Tell me all that, O you of noble vows, O treasure of mercy.

Mahādeva said: / For the sake of the welfare of his ancestors, he went to the snowy mountain; / having gone there, austerity was performed for ten thousand years.

The primeval deity, who is the spotless god, was pleased; / by him this Gaṅgā was granted, descending from the sky.

There the god Viśveśvara dwells perpetually; / having seen the Gaṅgā coming, the Jāhnavī was then received by him.

And having been held in the mass of his matted hair, she stayed for ten thousand years; / the Gaṅgā did not emerge then, solely due to the power of the Lord.

Then he wondered: “Where has my mother gone?” / Discerning thus through meditation, [he realized]: “She has indeed been captured by the Lord.”

Then that king Bhagīratha went to Kailāsa. / Having gone there, O best of sages, he performed fierce austerities.

Propitiated then by him, I gave the river. / Releasing a single strand of hair, the three-pathed river was then bestowed.

6.20.m:
Taking the Gaṅgā, he went to the netherworld where his ancestors were. / ‘Alakanandā’ was remembered as the first name of the Gaṅgā then.

When she reached Haridvāra, she was then the water from Viṣṇu’s foot. / That very ford is supreme, hard to attain even for the gods.

And having bathed at that sacred ford and especially beheld Hari, / those who perform circumambulation do not share in misery.

Multitudes of sins such as the killing of a brahmin are manifold; / they all vanish forever from the sight of Hari.

Once I went to Haridvāra, the abode of Keśava, / and from the power of that sacred ford, I became endowed with the form of Viṣṇu.

The best of men who go [there] attain indeed that painless state. / All those people—men and women alike—become four-armed.

They all go to Vaikuṇṭha merely by the sight of Hari. / Haridvāra, truly beautiful, is an even greater sacred ford to me.

It is the foremost sacred ford among sacred fords, bestowing the four aims of life, / granting dharma, wealth, and liberation to people in the Kali age,

where the greatly charming, pure Gaṅgā flows perpetually. / This is the holy, excellent narrative known as ‘Haridvāra.’
