6.20.m:
And when it is recited, an eternal reward accrues to the listeners, / equivalent to performing the horse sacrifice and gifting a thousand cows.

A wise man obtains that merit merely by the sight of Hari. / The slayer of a cow, the slayer of a brahmin, and whoever else are slayers of their fathers—

even many such sins of various kinds, O twice-born one, / all vanish merely by the sight of Hari.

6.22.m: Mahādeva said: / I shall declare the glorification of the Gaṅgā as it was spoken, O best of sages, / by merely hearing which sin is instantly destroyed.
Whoever says ‘Gaṅgā, Gaṅgā,’ even from hundreds of leagues away, / is freed from all sins and goes to the realm of Viṣṇu.
Sprung from the lotus-foot, she is renowned as the Gaṅgā, / and as the destroyer of dense masses of sins, O Nārada.
The Narmadā and the Sarayū, and likewise the Vetravatī river, / the Tāpī, the Payoṣṇī, the Candrā, the Vipāśā, the Karmanāśinī,
the Puṣyā, the Pūrṇā, likewise the Dīpā and the Vidīpā with the radiance of the sun: / whatever fruit one surely obtains from gifting a thousand bulls,
that fruit one attains instantly from the sight of the Gaṅgā. / This Gaṅgā is exceedingly holy, especially for those who have killed a brahmin;
for those consigned to hell, the Gaṅgā removes their sin. / And whatever fruit there is during an eclipse of the moon or the sun, O sinless one,
that fruit one attains merely by the sight of the Gaṅgā. / Just as darkness retreats far away at sunrise, my dear,
so sin vanishes through the power of the Gaṅgā. / She is ever revered in the world, pure, destroying sin,
always of auspicious form, created anciently by Viṣṇu. / She of divine form is considered a mother and a purifier of the wretched.
And as Viṣṇu is among the gods, so the Gaṅgā is the supreme river. / Men who bathe constantly during the month of Māgha—

no suffering exists for them for three hundred cosmic cycles. / Where the Gaṅgā and the Yamunā, and where the Sarasvatī indeed [meet], / having bathed and drunk there, one becomes a partaker of liberation; of this there is no doubt.

Mahādeva said: / Whatever I speak out of love for your news, O Lord, let that be praise of you; whatever I consume, let that be an offering to you; or wherever I go,
Whenever I sleep peacefully, let that be a prostration like a staff at the pair of your feet for us. / O Lord, whatever I do, let you, the Lord of the Universe, be pleased with that.
Beheld, worshipped, touched, or carried on the head— / which men are not liberated by that very water of the Yamunā?

Humans wander through the world, overcome by poverty, illness, death, and afflictions arising from worldly existence, / only as long as they do not behold your deep-dark blue water, O great river, nor place it upon their heads, O daughter of the Sun!

The mere recollection of whom instantly severs a flood of misdeeds; she who conquers a mass of sins even from a hundred thousand leagues away; / the repetition of whose name purifies the world—by good fortune, that very Gaṅgā will today come into the path of my sight!

By one yearning for the sight, with a mind full of joy, whose path was walked; in which [undertaking] the duty [is accomplished] at once, and now the foremost of fortunate men,
Bathing, the twilight ritual, libation, the worship of gods, and the feeding of brahmins at an ancestral rite—all this becomes complete and pleasing to the Lord; there is no wonder in this.

O Supreme Brahman transformed into a goddess, bestower of supreme bliss! / Accept my water-offering, O Gaṅgā; take away my sin; salutations to you!

the direct stream of liquefied dharma, the essence of the nectar of the lotus feet of the enemy of Mura, / a boat over the ocean of sorrow, praised by gods and men, the stairway leading to heaven,

carrying water that dispels all sins, radiant with a multitude of foremost qualities— / to that glorious Bhāgīrathī, O goddess, with a joyful mind I make my salutation.

O Heavenly River, who deliver people submerged in the ocean of sins, whose shimmering, / spotless radiant waves destroy the mass of darkness, O purifier of the world!

O divine Gaṅgā, purify me who am overcome by fear of misdeeds, a receptacle of compassion; / O Mother, protect me who have approached you for refuge, O giver of refuge, who am terrified by fear!

Ah, friend mind, why do you tremble? Are you terrified out of fear of hell? / Why do you fear, saying: "The scripture says a sinner becomes an inhabitant of hell"?

Do not fear! Listen to my path: even if a hell rivalling a mountain of sins / has been reached by me, what more is there? What wealth of righteousness do I not possess?

Where experiencing the joy of praising the Lord of all and others and bathing are prescribed, / seeing which the heavenly damsels and the wise lord of the gods are delighted by the prospect of gaining [the devotee].

In your water, O auspicious daughter of Jahnu, those devoted to restraints and observances who bathe / clearly attain godhood, even if they have done evil; the Vedas are the authority on this.

O intellect, may your wisdom be thus; friend mind, may all be well with you; / may you two feet always remain firm in this station, and you two eyes be fixed in pious vision!

O speech, beloved as my life, have a form of manifest virtue; attain the nourishment of living beings! / Because through all of you together I attain the peerless joy and the merit of the sacred ford.

O glorious Jāhnavī, daughter of the Sun, daughter of Brahmā! O ornament of the three rivers, supreme ford Prayāga! / O Lord of all, be gracious unto me, lead me upward to yourself, and shatter the ten-fold inner darkness with your splendour!

Whose dark-and-white bank even the Lord of Speech, Viṣṇu, Śiva, Indra, and others, the knowers among the knowers, / worship for the destruction of sin—victorious is that Prayāga, the king of sacred fords!

Where the heavenly river, reaching the confluence with the daughter of the sun and flowing westward, shakes off / the threefold spiritual affliction of humanity—victorious is Prayāga, king of sacred places!

Where the dark banyan tree, possessing the dark [deity's] qualities, covers people with its dark shade / and, when seen, cuts down the weariness of worldly existence—victorious is Prayāga, king of sacred places!
Where Brahmā and the gods, laying aside their own works, resort to that meritorious portion, / and where the rod-bearer [Yama] abandons his rod—victorious is Prayāga, king of sacred places!
Through whose service divine kings, gods, and celestial sages daily proclaim / heaven and the sovereignty over all the highest earth—victorious is Prayāga, king of sacred places!

By the power of whose name it is a known report that sins are destroyed, and glances [of grace] appear, / who has enveloped the three worlds with his rays [of light and waters]—victorious is Prayāga, king of sacred places!

Where the two noble white and dark rivers display all around the charming splendor of fly-whisks, / and the primeval banyan tree shines exceedingly like an umbrella—victorious is Prayāga, king of sacred places!

Where the Sarasvatī, the Yamunā, and the Gaṅgā, in the confluence of the three streams, by their very intact conjunction, / lead those who reach it to the station of Brahman—victorious is Prayāga, king of sacred places!

For some eloquent ones, ten million lifetimes pass, saying, "I will go, I will go," / and for some striving to reach it, an eminent number of years surely passes by.

that which is attained by hundreds of thousands of good fortunes—whether it happens or not—is beyond the reach of speech: / Prayāga, distinguished by the confluence, by fortune becomes a guest of sight to someone!

For people unable to perform sacrifices in the Kali age, who desire heaven through hymns, praises, / and verbal eulogies, how could they remain distressed with anxiety about attaining the immortal abode?

Having fully considered the fruit of complete sacrifices, headed by the Agniṣṭoma and the horse sacrifice, with their auxiliaries, / Brahmā and the other gods taught that this Prayāga alone, the king of sacred places, grants what is desired.

"Through the faults of negligence, distress, and the like, the rite of twilight devotion was not worshipped by me; / if one performs twilight worship here, through its grace may the twilight worship of my entire life become complete!"

Even elsewhere, he whose greatness is proclaimed in austerity, who is meditated upon with distant loves / and praised, bestows the desired station constantly without expecting anything in return.

to that glorious, incomparable Prayāga, lord of the confluence of the three streams, whose dust is holy, king of sacred places, / the best among the immortals, conscious, revealing the ornament of speech—to him I bow.

Was severe penance undergone by us? Ah, were sacrifices offered? / Were many kinds of gifts bestowed upon worthy recipients, or were the gods worshipped?

Was a true sacred place visited? Or was the assembly of twice-born honored with worship and the like, / by which the auspicious capital of Sadāśiva has been reached directly by itself?

Through the fortunes of many births, I have attained the city of Śiva, / destroyer of all sins, full of all wonders, a boat across the ocean of worldly existence.
The fruit of a noble birth has been obtained; the lineage has been sufficiently adorned; one's own self has been made pure; / and everything has been done—what else remains, standing above all?
"A living person sees a hundred thousand blessings"—since they speak thus not falsely, / therefore, even with such a body, fragile in a moment, Kāśī has indeed been reached by me!

Even the immortals on divine ground cannot accomplish the counting and worshipping of the true sacred places and liṅgas in Kāśī; / to those ancient, perfected ones, hidden and revealed here, with joined palms I bow.

What need of fear from hosts of sins? What need of rejoicing in countless merits performed? / What need of pride from study of knowledge, or despair from the fault of dullness?

What need of pride from the rise of wealth? What need of anguish from poverty, O people, / if Viśveśvara is seen after bathing in the waters of glorious Maṇikarṇikā?

With an unswollen, healthy, thin body, with clearly manifested capable self, with the strength rich in enthusiasm, alone,

that city of Gadādhara, which cannot be reached even by wishes, beyond the range even of the occurrence of dreams, / which bestows instantaneous liberation, has been attained!

I consider that it is neither one's own deed nor the power of attaining ancestors that brings this about; / nor is this fixed authority of one's own kin—so what of one's own afflictions and the like?
that attainment of Gayā, Prayāga, Yamunā, and Kāśī, hard to reach, which came through the arrival of the virtuous—there / the grace of glorious Śāradā, bringing great fruit, is victorious!

Who, even remembered from afar at the time of ancestral rites, gives liberation to the ancestors— / to that glorious Gadādhara, visibly present in Gayā, I bow.

Having crossed this path, difficult to traverse, exceedingly far from afar, teeming with small animals, tigers, hyenas, thorns, serpents, and adversaries,

having arrived, with meager speech, if a person begs for initial expenses, [holding] an earthen begging bowl: / "O glorious water-bearer Gadādhara, day after day he longs to see you!"

O Self of all, pleasing the gods with one's own vision and with the Gayā-śrāddha, / having made the universe without longing, how can you maintain indifference here?
Is this your constant pitilessness now? Or is it the sovereignty of the Kali age? Or is it an examination of sattva / for a long time among men? Or could it be a desire for [humble] service?
O Gadādhara, the ancestral rite has been performed by me through your grace; / permit me, O Lord, to return to my home!"
And the hymn of the four deities, which bestows heaven and wealth—whoever recites it constantly at the time of ancestral rites, and also at the time of bathing,

attains bathing equal to [bathing in] all sacred places from hearing, reciting, and chanting it. / From hearing the praise of Prayāga, Gaṅgā, and Yamunā, O twice-born one, / faults born of karma are destroyed.

6.23.m: Mahādeva said: / Listen, O Nārada, I will tell the glorification originating from Tulasī, / hearing which one is freed from sin from birth until the end of death.
Leaf, flower, fruit, root, branch, bark, and stem— / everything produced from Tulasī is purifying, as are its soil and the rest.
Those whose body is burned by fire of Tulasī wood— / and having placed Tulasī wood on all the limbs of the deceased,
he who subsequently performs the cremation is also freed from sin. / He who, at death, has obtained the chanting and remembering of Hari,
and cremation with Tulasī wood—for him there is no return [to rebirth]. / If there is even one stick of Tulasī wood in the midst of a hundred sticks of wood,
at the time of cremation, liberation is obtained, even for one with tens of millions of sins. / Just as [waters] attain holiness through consecration with Gaṅgā water,
so pieces of wood mixed with Tulasī wood attain holiness. / As long as the funeral pyre mixed with Tulasī wood burns,
so long his sins committed throughout tens of millions of cosmic ages are burned away. / Seeing a man being burned by the fire of Tulasī wood,
the messengers of Viṣṇu lead him, not the servants of Yama. / Liberated from thousands of tens of millions of births, he goes to Janārdana.
Those men in the world who are burned by the fire of Tulasī wood— / the gods, standing in celestial chariots, scatter handfuls of flowers upon them.
All the apsarases dance; singers sing songs; / Viṣṇu, seeing him, becomes pleased, together with Śambhu.
Taking him by the hand, Śauri leads him home, and from his body / wipes away all sins while the dwellers of heaven watch.
Having arranged a great festival preceded by cries of victory, / wherever the fire of tulasī wood blazes with clarified butter,

in the fire-house or in the cremation ground, the sin of men is burned. / Whatever brāhmaṇas perform a fire-offering with fire from tulasī wood, / with each sprinkled sesame seed they obtain the fruit of an Agniṣṭoma sacrifice.
Whoever offers incense to Hari produced from tulasī wood / attains merit equal to a hundred sacrifices and the fruit of a hundred cows.
The food offering that is cooked with fire from tulasī wood / becomes equal to Mount Meru when offered to Keśava.
Furthermore, whoever lights a lamp for Hari with tulasī fire / obtains the meritorious fruit of a hundred thousand lamps.
No one equal to him is seen on earth among Vaiṣṇavas / who offers tulasī-wood paste to Kṛṣṇa.
He becomes a vessel of Viṣṇu's grace, O best of brāhmaṇas.
Having anointed Hari with devotion in the Kali age using paste made from tulasī wood, / he rejoices eternally in the presence of Hari.
One whose limbs are anointed with tulasī paste performs the worship of Viṣṇu; / through a single day's worship, the fruit of a hundred days and a hundred cows is obtained.
As long as tulasī-wood paste for anointing Kṛṣṇa / remains in the temple, listen to the fruit of that merit:
The merit that a man would obtain by giving eight prasthas of sesame, / that same fruit arises for men through the grace of the wielder of the discus.
Whoever gives an offering-ball to the ancestors containing a tulasī leaf, / for leaf after leaf, satisfaction lasting a hundred years is produced.
One should especially bathe with the clay from the root of a tulasī; / by him a bath is taken at a holy place as long as the clay is on his limbs.
Whoever performs worship with its flower-spike / has performed worship with various flowers as long as the moon and sun endure.
In whatever house a garden of tulasī plants stands, / sins such as the slaying of a brāhmaṇa, through seeing and touching, / all dissolve by merely seeing it, O Nārada.
Mahādeva said: / Now I shall tell you another thing; listen with a one-pointed mind. / It has not been told to anyone; listen, O best of divine sages.
Wherever a tulasī is present—in a house, a village, or a forest— / there Hari, the Lord of the world, dwells with a delighted soul.
In that house there is no poverty, no separation from relatives, / no sorrow, no fear, and no disease where tulasī stands.
Everywhere tulasī is auspicious, especially in a sacred place, / through being planted upon the surface of the earth in the presence of that deity.

For them, the abode of Viṣṇu is eternal once the planting of tulasī is done. / Fierce calamities, diseases, and numerous bad omens / Hari destroys, bringing peace, when worshipped with devotion through tulasī.
Wherever the wind blows carrying the fragrance of tulasī, / the ten directions are purified, as is the fourfold multitude of living beings.
In whatever house, O best of sages, the clay from the root of a tulasī is kept, / the gods, Śiva, and Hari dwell there at all times.
Wherever the shadow of a grove of tulasī falls, O sky-born one, / whoever offers a libation there gives what is imperishable to the ancestors.
At its root sits Brahmā, in the middle the god Janārdana, / and in the flower-spike dwells Rudra; therefore tulasī is purifying.
Whoever performs purification at twilight without tulasī, / all of that is stolen by rākṣasas and leads him to hell.
Whoever bears upon his head water dripping from a tulasī leaf / obtains the fruit of the Gaṅgā and gains the fruit of a hundred cows.
If one should plant tulasī especially in a temple of Śiva, / he will dwell in heaven for each single seed according to the number of cosmic ages.
By Umā formerly, O goddess, for the sake of Śaṅkara on the Himālayas, / a hundred plants of tulasī were planted; to them I bow down.
Whoever plants it on the occasion of a festival, in the month of Śrāvaṇa, / or on the day of a solar transit—tulasī gives exceedingly great merit.
One should worship tulasī daily; a poor man becomes a master. / It is a form that brings all accomplishments, and Kṛṣṇa grants renown.
Where a Śālagrāma stone is present, there Hari is near at hand; / bathing and gifting there are a hundred times superior to Vārāṇasī.
From the worship of a Śālagrāma stone arises merit ten-million-fold greater / than Kurukṣetra, Prayāga, and the Naimiṣa Forest.
Wherever the sacred sign of a Śālagrāma is situated, / whatever merit there is in Vārāṇasī, all of it is found right there.
Whatever sin a man commits, such as the slaying of a brāhmaṇa, / he destroys all of it quickly through the worship of a Śālagrāma stone.

6.24.m: Mahādeva said: / I shall proclaim the glorification of the holy place Prayāga as it has been heard, / where there are people devoted to great giving and perform virtuous deeds.
Where the Gaṅgā, the Yamunā, and the Sarasvatī are present— / that best among divine holy places is hard to reach even for the gods.
Nothing such has existed or will exist in the three worlds. / Just as the sun is among the planets and the moon among the asterisms,
so is the holy place named Prayāga, the unexcelled best among holy places. / In the morning, O wise one, one should bathe in Prayāga.
Freed from great sin, he goes to the supreme abode. / Something should be given according to one's means by one who desires the destruction of poverty.
Whatever man goes there and bathes in Prayāga / becomes wealthy and long-lived; of this there is no doubt.
Where a man gazes upon the imperishable banyan tree, / by that mere sight the slaying of a brāhmaṇa is destroyed.
And it is known as the imperishable banyan tree; it is seen even at the end of a cosmic age. / Viṣṇu sleeps on its leaf; therefore it is remembered as imperishable.
Men who are dear to Viṣṇu perform worship there; / having covered it with a thread, one should perform worship.
The deity named Mādhava constantly dwells there happily; / one must behold him, and one is freed from great sins.
Where the gods, sages, and mortals on every side, / having taken recourse to their respective places, constantly dwell.
Even a killer of cows, an outcaste, an evil person, or one of wicked mind, / a slayer of children, or an ignorant man, if he dies right there,
he indeed becomes four-armed and dwells in Vaikuṇṭha for a long time. / And whatever man performs the bath of the month of Māgha at Prayāga,
there is no reckoning of his fruit; listen, O best of divine sages. / The waters are called 'nārāḥ', so we have heard in all the worlds;
therefore Nārāyaṇa is proclaimed, grantor of enjoyment and liberation to those who bathe. / Just as the sun is among the planets and the moon among the asterisms,
so is Māgha best among months for all religious acts. / When the sun is in Capricorn, in the month of Māgha, in the pure morning hour,
bathing even in water measuring a cow's footprint grants heaven even to sinners. / This conjunction is rare, O wise one, in the three worlds with all that moves and is motionless.
Whoever, having made the effort during this time, should bathe for even three days, / or five, or seven, taking the bath originating at Prayāga,
he too prospers like the moon in his lineage, O best of Brahmins. / And whatever living beings there are, moving and unmoving, human beings and the rest,
taking refuge in the sacred site of Prayāga, they soon go to Vaikuṇṭha. / Those who are the sages there, Vasiṣṭha and others, Sanaka and others,
they too resort repeatedly to the sacred site born of Prayāga. / Where Viṣṇu and Rudra are, and where Indra is also,
all of them reside here in Prayāga, the best of sacred sites. / They praise gifts given there, and likewise the observances;
having bathed there and having drunk [its water], there is no rebirth.

6.25.m: Nārada said: / Thus has the glorification of Tulasī been heard by me through your grace; / now tell of the three-night Tulasī vow.
Sadāśiva said: / Hear, O Brahmin of great intellect, this ancient vow, / hearing which one is freed from all sins, there is no doubt about this.
Formerly, in the Raibhyantara kalpa, there was a king, a lord of subjects; / and his wife was renowned as Candrarūpā, a deeply faithful wife.
She indeed performed this vow, which grants the fruits of all desires; / and her three-night vow granted dharma, desire, wealth, and liberation.
Fruitful is the life of those by whom the Tulasī vow has been heard. / In the bright fortnight of Kārttika, on the ninth day, O Nārada,
abiding by the observances, the vow-keeper should remain sleeping on the ground with senses conquered. / Dedicated to the three-night vow, pure, with a restrained mind,
he should sleep, observing the rules, near a grove of Tulasī. / Then, at midday, in pure water in a river or the like,
having bathed, he should make libations to the ancestors and the gods according to rule. / He should have a golden image made of the god Janārdana together with Lakṣmī.

No miserliness regarding wealth should be committed by one desiring his own welfare. / Then a pair of garments should be provided, yellow or white robes, / [and] the propitiation of the nine planets should be commenced according to rule.
Having cooked the sacrificial offering there, he should perform the Vaiṣṇava oblations. / On the twelfth day, having carefully worshipped the lord of gods,
he should install an unblemished, pure water pot according to rule, / furnished with five jewels, with sprouts and endowed with herbs.
Upon it, in a vessel, he should place Janārdana together with Lakṣmī. / He should install [it] at the root of a Tulasī plant with Vedic and Purāṇic mantras.
He should sprinkle the Tulasī grove with milk alone. / Having bathed the god of gods, the guru of the universe, with the five nectars,

'He who has endless forms, who is all-universe-formed, in the waters of the womb sustains the cosmic order, / may he, that god of gods, be pleased with me, who through his māyā is the maker of the universe, and this goddess.' / [Prayer mantra]
'Come, O Acyuta, lord of gods, mass of splendor, lord of the world! / Ever the destroyer of darkness, protect me from the ocean of worldly existence!' / [Invocation mantra]
'With a good bath of five nectars, and with perfumed water, / and with the water of the Gaṅgā and other rivers, bathed, may the Infinite One be pleased.' / [Bathing mantra]
'Sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, saffron, and other ointments, / offered by me with devotion, O god, together with Lakṣmī, do receive!' / [Anointing mantra]
'Nārāyaṇa, reverence to you, deliverer from the ocean of hell, / sovereign of the three worlds, to you I give two auspicious garments!' / [Garment mantra]
'Dāmodara, reverence to you! Save me from the ocean of worldly existence! / The sacred thread is offered by me; accept it, O Supreme Person!' / [Sacred-thread mantra]
'And fragrant flowers, mālatī and others indeed, O Lord, / have been offered by me, O lord of gods; let them be graciously accepted!' / [Flower mantra]
'May the food offering be accepted, O Lord, furnished with edible delicacies and dishes, / richly endowed with all flavors; accept it, O Supreme Lord!' / [Food-offering mantra]
'Areca nuts, betel leaves, and together with camphor, / have been offered by me, O lord of gods; let the betel preparation be accepted!' / [Betel mantra]
Having offered incense of aloe and guggulu mixed with ghee with devotion, / in this manner worship is to be performed; he should present a lamp with ghee.
Having arranged various lamps, O tiger among sages, collected in mind, / in front of Lakṣmīnārāyaṇa, near the Tulasī grove,
an offering of water and honor is to be presented there to the god of gods, the wielder of the discus: / on the ninth day with a coconut for the sake of obtaining a son—an excellent offering—
on the tenth day with a citron for the attainment of dharma, desire, and wealth, / on the eleventh day with a pomegranate, he will forever destroy poverty.
Endowed with seven grains, in a bamboo vessel, O Nārada, / accompanied by seven fruits, with leaves and areca nuts,
having covered it with a cloth, he should present it before the god / with this mantra, O foremost of Brahmins; hear with a single-pointed mind:
'O god accompanied by Tulasī, ever joined with the conch, / receive the offering given by me, O god of gods, reverence to you!' / [Offering mantra]
Having thus worshipped the lord of gods, Janārdana together with Lakṣmī, / he should pray to the god of gods for the successful completion of the vow:
'I have fasted, O lord of gods, free from desire and anger; / through this vow, O lord of gods, you alone are my refuge.
In this vow undertaken, O god, whatever has been done incompletely by me, / may all that become complete through your grace, O Janārdana.
Reverence, O lotus-petal-eyed one! Reverence to you who sleep on the waters! / This vow has been performed by me through your grace, O Keśava.
O destroyer of the darkness of ignorance, through this vow, O Keśava, / becoming benevolent with grace, be the giver of the vision of knowledge!'
Then there is a vigil at night, with singing and recitation of books, / with experts in sound, dance, and arts, and with very auspicious holy narratives.
When the night has dawned and the clear sun has risen, / having invited Brahmins with devotion, he should perform a Vaiṣṇava funeral feast.
Having fed them as they desire with milk rice and ghee, / along with betel, flowers, fragrances, and the like, accompanied by priestly gifts,
having given sacred threads, garments, garlands, and sandalwood, / three married couples should be fed, [honored] with garments, ornaments, and saffron.
He should fill bamboo vessels according to his means with sprouted grains, / and with coconuts, cooked foods, garments, and various fruits.
There he should clothe the guru accompanied by his wife with garments, / and worship him with heavenly ornaments, fragrances, and garlands.
And he should give a milch cow equipped with all furnishings, / accompanied by a priestly gift and with cloth; hear that as I declare it:
Whatever merit arises for men who have bathed in all sacred sites, / all that fruit he obtains through the grace of the god of gods.
And having enjoyed extensive pleasures, all delightful desires, / he attains the Vaiṣṇava realm at the end, through the grace of Viṣṇu.

6.26.m: Nārada said: / When a man desires to give gifts to Brahmins superior in virtue, / what things should he give in this world? Tell all that accordingly.

Mahādeva said:
Having understood the truth in the world, listen, best of divine sages: / Thus they praise food alone; everything is established upon food.
Therefore people especially desire to give food. / There never was nor ever will be a gift equal to food.
By food the universe, the world of the moving and unmoving, is sustained. / Food gives vigor in the world, and life-breaths are indeed established on food.
Edible food should indeed be given to a noble brāhmaṇa / even by afflicting one's family, if one desires one's own prosperity.
O Nārada, he is the best of the wise who gives food to a petitioner, / to an afflicted brāhmaṇa, for his own other-worldly benefit.
One who desires one's own prosperity should attend at the proper time to a twice-born guest who has arrived, / tired, returning on his way, coming to a householder's house.
A wise giver of food, virtuous and free from malice, / having set aside arisen anger, attains whatever happiness [there is] in heaven and here.
He should not disparage a guest, nor should he ever bear ill-will; / he should offer food to a knower of the Veda, and that gift is distinguished.
He who gives to an exhausted person not seen before, returning along a path, / deeply distressed, attains all merit.
The man who pleases the ancestors, the gods, the vipras, and guests with food, / O great sage, his merit is infinite.
Even having committed a very great sin, he who gives food to a supplicant, / especially to a brāhmaṇa, is indeed freed from sins.
A gift to brāhmaṇas is imperishable; food given to a śūdra yields great fruit. / The giving of food is commended both to a śūdra and to a brāhmaṇa.
One should not ask his lineage, conduct, or Vedic study; / here a mendicant is indeed a brāhmaṇa: one should give food, and he departs.
For the giver of food, auspicious trees yielding all desired fruits / arise in this world and, full of joy, in heaven.
Hear of those worlds attained by the gift of food, O great sage: / aerial cars shine in heaven for those noble beings;
of various designs and forms, equipped with various desired objects, / and trees yielding all desired fruits situated in their abode;
all kinds of auspicious golden stepped wells and elongated ponds everywhere, / and resonant vehicles unloosened by the thousands;
mountains consisting of pastries and cooked food, garments and ornaments, / rivers flowing with milk, and likewise mountains of clarified butter;
mansions shining with a white luster, and beds resplendent with gold. / They desire to give that food; therefore one should become a giver of food.
These worlds belong to the performers of meritorious deeds; the gift of food has great fruit. / Therefore, food must especially be given by mortals on earth.
